title: Jim Callaghan's Secret Garden, Fifty Years On
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou uses the fiftieth anniversary of Jim Callaghan's 1976 'Secret Garden' speech to trace the history of central government accountability in British education and draw lessons for Andy Burnham's devolution agenda. Callaghan's speech broke a postwar taboo by suggesting elected politicians had a legitimate interest in what schools taught—a position so inflammatory that a head teachers' union compared it to Nazi curriculum interference. Despite generating no legislation, the speech helped establish the intellectual foundation for the 1988 National Curriculum. Christodoulou identifies three forces that drove the consensus toward centralization: international economic competition, visible local management failures, and fiscal tensions between central funding and local authority control. She warns that devolution without commensurate tax-raising powers risks recreating the same dysfunctional accountability muddle that Callaghan diagnosed fifty years ago.
points: Callaghan's 1976 'Secret Garden' speech challenged a postwar taboo in which curriculum was considered beyond democratic accountability—a position so controversial that critics compared it to Nazi interference.
Despite producing no legislation, the speech laid intellectual groundwork for the 1988 Education Reform Act and a national curriculum that has persisted across all subsequent governments.

Three forces drove the shift toward centralization: global economic competition exposing British complacency, visible local failures like the William Tyndale affair, and fiscal tensions between central funding and local authority decision-making.
The structural problem then—and now—is that funding flows from central government while control rests locally, creating unclear lines of accountability that allow both sides to blame each other.
Christodoulou warns that Andy Burnham's devolution agenda risks repeating the same mistake unless local authorities gain genuine tax-raising powers alongside devolved responsibilities.
quotes: It is known as the 'Secret Garden' speech because Callaghan compared the world of education to a secret garden that elected politicians, parents and ordinary taxpayers were not allowed to have an opinion on, even when things were obviously going wrong.

Even that circumlocutory phrasing was inflammatory, and was enough to bring out the 'continental tyranny' counter argument: the general secretary of the head teachers' union compared the proposal to Nazi interference in the 1930s German curriculum.

Callaghan's speech was just a speech, and wasn't followed up by any legislation on curriculum. It was enormously influential and was frequently cited 12 years later when the Conservative government passed the landmark 1988 Education Reform Act.
It was always going to be unsustainable for education to receive so much funding from central government, but for central government to have so little say over it.

The lesson from the past is that if you devolve power and responsibility without commensurate tax-raising powers, you get problems. You risk getting irresponsible local authorities, and a meddlesome central government.
